title: Social Cognition in Forensic Psychology
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines principles of social cognition in forensic psychology, a field that sits at the intersection of psychological science and the justice system. Social cognition—the study of how people perceive, interpret, and respond to others—rests on four pillars: impression formation, stereotypes and prejudice, attribution, and attitudes. Much of forensic psychology, from competency evaluations to risk assessments to testimony about eyewitness identification accuracy, implicitly involves these social‐cognitive processes. Rather than a comprehensive review, this paper draws selectively on material chosen to highlight key ideas and to stimulate further reading and discourse. To that end, we present three illustrative concepts of social cognition relevant to forensic contexts: (1) disruptions in social cognition can have forensic significance, (2) social perception in legal settings is dynamic and reciprocal, and (3) evaluating expert witness testimony is especially difficult. Within legal processes, judges, jurors, attorneys, parties to the case (e.g., defendants, plaintiffs), and witnesses engage in social‐cognitive dynamics that shape how justice unfolds. Heuristics—such as judging credibility based on likeability, fluency, or attractiveness—can distort accuracy of perceptions. Accordingly, awareness of social‐cognitive influences may be particularly important in forensic settings, where judgments about individuals can have significant implications for legal outcomes. Throughout the paper, we offer a comparative reflection of overlapping concepts from social cognition and forensic psychology, highlighting underexplored connections and future directions for research and teaching. Comparative work like this has potential to generate scientific advancements, to the benefit of basic theoretical breakthroughs and enduring solutions for applied problems.
